planting.note: Set out young trees in spring on sandy, acidic, or poor soils where this tough pioneer species readily colonizes abandoned fields and roadsides.

directions: Set out young trees in spring on sandy, acidic, or poor soils where this tough pioneer species readily colonizes abandoned fields and roadsides. Its slender, chalky-white trunks with black triangular patches beneath each branch and its fine-textured, fluttering foliage give it strong ornamental value in multi-stem clumps. Gray birch tolerates poor drainage and infertile ground better than paper birch but is shorter-lived, typically thriving for only 30-50 years, making it best suited to naturalized or reclamation plantings rather than a long-term specimen. It requires little supplemental water once established, unlike its moisture-loving birch relatives.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown trees in spring near stream banks, drainage swales, or large open lawns where this thirsty, wide-spreading root system has room to run.

directions: Transplant container-grown trees in spring near stream banks, drainage swales, or large open lawns where this California and Southwest native's thirsty, wide-spreading roots have room to run. Its mottled, exfoliating white-and-tan bark and massive, often multi-trunked, gnarled form make it a dramatic focal point in western landscapes and riparian restoration projects. Large maple-like leaves provide heavy dappled shade in summer, and the tree tolerates seasonal flooding as well as the region's dry summers once its roots reach groundwater. Provide supplemental irrigation for the first several years until the tree is deep-rooted and self-sufficient.

planting.note: Plant in spring along desert washes, canyon bottoms, or irrigated landscape zones that mimic its native riparian habitat in southern Arizona and New Mexico canyons.

directions: Plant in spring along desert washes, canyon bottoms, or irrigated landscape zones that mimic its native riparian habitat in southern Arizona and New Mexico canyons. Deeply cut, palmate leaves and smooth white upper bark give it striking form against arid backdrops, while its multi-trunked, twisting habit develops character with age. This sycamore provides critical shade and nesting habitat for desert wildlife along streamcourses and tolerates the region's intense summer heat as long as its roots have access to subsurface moisture. Water deeply and infrequently during establishment to encourage the deep rooting this species depends on in the wild.

planting.note: Plant in consistently wet, poorly drained sites such as swamp edges, floodplains, or low spots; seed requires warm then cold stratification and often germinates in its second spring.

directions: Plant in consistently wet, poorly drained sites such as swamp edges, floodplains, or low spots where few other shade trees tolerate standing water for extended periods. Compound leaves with 7-11 leaflets turn a soft yellow in fall, and the tree's flexible wood was historically prized by indigenous basket weavers for splint material. Black ash is highly susceptible to emerald ash borer, so it is now best planted only in restoration or wetland mitigation contexts with active pest monitoring. Choose a site with year-round soil moisture, since this species does not tolerate drought.

planting.note: Set out young trees in fall on dry limestone slopes or upland alkaline soils; shows somewhat greater tolerance to emerald ash borer than other native ashes.

directions: Set out young trees in fall on dry limestone slopes or upland alkaline soils, where its distinctive four-angled, winged young twigs and thick corky bark set it apart from other native ashes. This species shows somewhat greater tolerance to emerald ash borer than other North American ashes, making it a more resilient choice for restoration and specimen plantings where ash trees are otherwise declining. Its dense, rounded canopy provides good shade for dry, calcareous sites that few large shade trees can handle. Historically its inner bark sap was boiled down to produce a blue dye, giving the species its common name.
